column79: Apretando tuercas y tornillos —tightening the nuts and bolts—a seemingly mundane task with extraordinary implications. When I was four, I worked alongside my abuelo to craft a water-well-shaped planter for my abuela. Still there today, a little tattered, the planter overflows with fragrant tulips and dainty forget-me-nots. Seeing my abuela’s smile at our tangible creation sparked a drive in me to create things that leave a lasting mark on the world. Growing up in Chicago, I witnessed how architecture can shape a community. From the towering skyscrapers of the South Loop to the vibrant murals in Pilsen, the city’s design reflects the collaborative efforts of engineers, architects, and residents. However, I've also seen how design often fails to meet the needs of underserved communities. In neighborhoods like my abuela’s, where buildings lack energy-efficient infrastructure, high utility costs burden residents. This gap drives me to use engineering as a tool to create sustainable and inclusive solutions that address both technical and social challenges, ensuring that all communities benefit from well-designed spaces. To translate this vision into reality, my experience with the Chicago Association of Student Engineers (CASE) has reinforced the importance of teamwork and clear communication in creating impactful, community-focused solutions. As co-president, I helped grow our outreach, organize networking events, and establish partnerships with engineering firms. Through these experiences, I discovered my passion for project management: leading teams, managing logistics, and ensuring we achieve our goals while fostering a supportive community. Throughout my STEM journey, it's been frustrating to often be one of the few Latinas in the room. Through Girls Build! I’ve learned the importance of diverse perspectives to incite real change while growing alongside a community of like-minded women ready to change the world. Now, as a Junior Board Member of Girls Build!, I help design the curriculum and mentor girls passionate about design in our sessions. My experience has taught me how to demystify design for myself and others and shown me the power of creating opportunities that encourage diverse perspectives. The culmination of these experiences has solidified my desire to lead projects that address the needs of diverse communities, bringing sustainable solutions to the forefront of design. By combining my interpersonal skills with my passion for STEM, I am eager to work at the intersection of business and engineering to spearhead interdisciplinary teams that build infrastructure that’s not only innovative, but also accessible and inclusive. At UC Berkeley, I know I’ll gain the technical expertise and business acumen to turn these ideas into impactful, tangible solutions. I’m excited to create a sustainable future while uplifting diverse voices along the way. Un tornillo a la vez —one bolt at a time.

column79: At age four, I was diagnosed with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), a rare blood disorder that causes my body to mistakenly attack its platelets, the cells that form clots to stop bleeding. While the average person has more than 150,000 platelets, I had only 5,000. The tiniest push would leave dark bruises on my fragile body. No playground games, no contact sports, no riding a bike. Nothing. While my physical activity was constrained, my intellectual curiosity grew limitless. At every doctor’s visit, I asked endless questions about my condition: What do platelets do? What biological pathways triggered my immune system’s platelet response? Why did my antibodies mistake platelets as invaders and not allies? This relentless curiosity followed me into high school, where I embraced challenging STEM classes and fell in love with the field’s potential to solve pressing challenges and unravel the intricate workings of what we call life . I believe the future of our world lies within engineering, as the rapid rise of mind-blowing innovations—like NVIDIA’s AI Chips, CRISPR gene editing, and da Vinci robotic surgery—has already begun to change the ways humans exist in their daily lives. At every moment, researchers everywhere are racing to join this booming revolution. My sister posed an amusing question to me the other day: “Would you rather be coded for, or would you rather be the one coding?” In college, I plan to pursue a double major in bioengineering and computer science, which will give me a strong foundation to discover my own path towards an engineering career. I aspire to be a medical researcher, specifically working to advance cures for blood disorders. Through my experiences of being a chronic blood disorder patient and recently losing my grandmother to locked-in syndrome from multiple strokes, I’ve gained a deeper understanding of the urgency behind medical advancements. College provides a launchpad for me to push the boundaries of what’s possible. I’m excited to apply what I learn in mind-opening classes to collaborative research, prototyping new medical devices and brainstorming the next big thing with fellow passion-driven innovators. One of my main goals is to conduct a project that transforms immunotherapy cures for ITP by investigating its cellular pathways and root causes with AI machine-learning. Beyond research, I am committed to inspiring the next generation of young engineers, because it takes a village to create change and improve lives across the globe. During my internship with InspiroGram, I’ve had the opportunity to work with people of all backgrounds towards our mission of introducing coding to students in developing countries. In college, I strive to continue this movement by launching an initiative that partners with organizations worldwide, bringing accessible education in technology and engineering to communities struggling to keep up in this rapidly modernizing world. Through my education and career in engineering, I hope to bridge the gap between research and real-world impact—harnessing the power of computing to drive healthcare forward and forge breakthroughs in hematology that help people with chronic disorders like me.

column79: A month before my birth, the discovery of Gliese 581c set the scientific community aflame with excitement over the most Earth-like planet yet observed. Before I turned one, they had already moved on to studying its neighbor, Gliese 581d. I’m driven towards physics by this relentless push to unveil the universe's secrets. As I break down problems into their components, I simplify a situation’s complexity into the fundamental laws that define it. The struggle always leads to a rewarding solution – or at least an interesting dead-end. Studying physics is a chance to immerse myself in numerical analysis without venturing too close to the dizzying space of pure math, and take advantage of computer science without losing touch of good-old paper and pencil. I’m particularly interested in spending my life tackling environmental issues. My personal experiences and academic exploration have highlighted the disproportionate impact of climate change on low-income countries and coastal regions. I hope to lead the charge in adapting and protecting these vulnerable regions from further trauma and loss. In addition to a major in engineering physics, I’m planning to minor in Environment and Sustainability. The unique electives offered within the minor at MIT, from “Economic Systems” to “Materials and Material Culture”, will help me address specific niches that may be overlooked today. After my undergraduate education, I plan to pursue graduate school to earn a P.h.D. in an interdisciplinary program focused on climate resilience. I hope to develop innovative and sustainable technologies that enable widespread societal shifts away from exploitation of the resources around us. My research experiences at Fermilab and UNC-Chapel Hill have taught me the importance of approaching such large-scale problems with the engineering mindset: starting with fundamental principles and allowing creative thinking to forge a path forward. Alongside my academic research, I hope to collaborate with policymakers and local organizations to ensure that the solutions I create are accessible and effective in regions that need them the most. As a co-captain of my school’s policy debate team and competitor for the last seven years, I’ve developed a deep understanding of how governments and policy reforms are structured. I’ll continue to build upon this by collaborating with grassroots efforts to raise awareness, signing petitions to promote stronger regulations, and lobbying for climate initiatives. I know the world needs to dream big to address the climate issue and actualize ideas like nuclear energy and net-zero transportation. Whether at a research lab like the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center or an envirotech startup that I create myself, I will fight to ensure that humanity is treating the world in sustainable ways.

At Trinity College , I look forward to participating in more opportunities like this. As a Mechanical Major, I could learn more about 3D printing through prototyping workshops offered there. Such examples drive home the point that thoughtful, well-engineered systems can mitigate human error and bias, ensuring that safety and efficiency are never sacrificed for short-term gains. My desire to become a software engineer stems from this understanding. Faulty software and maintenance failures have been linked to catastrophic errors in industries like aviation, showing how engineers have an immense responsibility when designing systems that affect countless lives. This task isn’t just about numbers, it represents the blend of technical rigor and creative problem-solving essential to engineering. Even the 19th-century English Luddites, who demolished machinery out of fear that new technologies would replace their skills, serve as a potent reminder of the human side of technological progress. Their actions emphasize the importance of designing innovations that advance efficiency and consider societal impacts. With an engineering degree, I will be equipped to develop software that streamlines operations, enhances safety, and ultimately improves quality of life. Whether by building platforms that empower communities or creating systems that prevent costly errors in critical infrastructure, I envision a career where my work leaves a lasting, positive impact on the world. column79: From a young age, I was captivated by how the world works, particularly the chemistry behind everything. At five, I mixed potions in the bathtub, imagining potions that could make me into a mermaid or ten feet tall. At ten, I disassembled old tablets and toys, eager to understand how they worked. My fascinations drew me towards STEM, as I realized it held the key to understanding the universe. However, I soon found myself part of an obscure minority: women in STEM. In elementary school, the gender gap in science didn’t seem obvious. Everyone participated in the yearly science fair, making elephant toothpaste or baking soda volcanoes without questioning who belonged. But as I entered middle school at Brooks, I noticed a divide in my advanced classes. By high school, the gender imbalance in my AP and dual credit STEM courses became even more pronounced. Despite female students outnumbering males at my school, STEM classes remained male-dominated. It wasn’t just the numbers that bothered me, it was the expectations. My school seemed to assume boys would excel in STEM while girls were overlooked. In my junior-year honors physics class, this reality became painfully clear. My group, mostly boys, was assigned an egg drop project. Eager to innovate, I proposed creative solutions, only to be dismissed. Some contributed nothing, expecting me to “prove” myself, while others doubted my abilities entirely. Their skepticism dimmed my confidence but ignited a new fire within me. Instead of backing down, I took charge, designing and executing the project myself. That experience shaped me into a leader, teaching me resilience and self-reliance. Alongside academic struggles, I battled the societal pressure that my appearance would overshadow my intellect. In high school, where looks often dictate your social lI've, I constantly struggled to prove that beauty and intelligence can coexist. Too often, I felt reduced to a “pretty face,” as if my contributions were secondary to my appearance. Christina Yang from Grey’s Anatomy put it best: “Screw beauty. I’m brilliant.” I embrace this mindset as I pursue biomedical engineering, determined to break barriers for women like me. My passion for making a difference grows each day, especially when I reflect on my Aunt Janetta’s battle with cancer. Watching her fight, I wished medicine had been advanced enough to save her. Her struggle fuels my drive to improve healthcare technology so families no longer have to hear, “Sorry, there’s nothing else we can do.” Just as I once created potions to transform the ordinary, I now aim to craft real solutions in biomedical engineering, revolutionizing healthcare for families worldwide. My passion also stems from my aunt Janetta’s battle with cancer, where I wished medicine could've been advanced enough to save her. Her fight inspired me to seek ways to improve healthcare through engineering, so that “ sorry, there’s nothing else we can do” never has to be heard again. I’ve learned that gender does not define ability, instead passion and perseverance do. So, screw beauty. Be brilliant.

Alongside my creative pursuits, I have always had a deep appreciation for STEM. As a shy and socially awkward individual, art and science became my primary means of communication and expression. A transformative moment in my journey was being selected as a collegiate scholar at the University of Chicago, where I explored the practical applications of STEM beyond the classroom. This experience reshaped my perspective. engineering was no longer just a subject; it was a tool to solve real-world problems. I coded a robot to respond to light, envisioning its potential integration into solar panel technology. I also designed an experiment using EMG equipment with the Rubber Hand Illusion to investigate how sensory feedback and proprioception influence the brain’s perception of body ownership. These experiences solidified my passion for engineering. Two years ago, I published a literature review on the impact of microplastics (MPs) on human health and presented my findings at the Annual Conference on Adolescent Health. What I learned was alarming and deepened my commitment to addressing an issue that has been largely overlooked in our reliance on plastic products. Nearly a century after the mass production of plastics began, yet only 9% of it is recycled. The rest accumulates in landfills or pollutes natural ecosystems. Microplastics, plastic fragments smaller than 5 mm, are now pervasive in the environment, from Arctic snow to the deepest ocean trenches. Even more concerning, they have been detected in human blood, lungs, liver, and placentas. While the full extent of their impact on human health is still being studied, we already know that MPs can release toxic additives such as PFAS, BPA, and phthalates—chemicals linked to developmental delays, cardiovascular disease, asthma, and endocrine disruption, especially in children. Recognizing the urgency of this crisis, I became committed to finding solutions. I chose to pursue a degree in Bioengineering or Biochemical Engineering, aiming to develop sustainable packaging alternatives and mitigation strategies for microplastic pollution. My ambition is to earn a PhD in Engineering and leverage my expertise as a scientist and entrepreneur to develop sustainable solutions that protect both human health and the environment. Through engineering, I aim to bridge science and creativity to address one of the most pressing environmental challenges of our time.

column79: Looking back, I never would have guessed badminton would be the ignitor for my passion in biomechical engineering. Specifically, my passions for accessibility started when I had abruptly torn my ACL in an intense badminton game. Initially, I was drowned in the devastating fact that I could no longer play my favorite sport. Quickly, that devastation turned into frustration and despair. The overwhelming medical bills for orthopedic visits, physical therapy sessions, surgery, and my work absences had become an ignitor to my passions for accessibility. During my rehabilitation process, I saw a cryotherapy machine for the first time. Fascinated by its compact yet innovative system I wanted to know: How could it circulate cold water continuously? How could this machine be preventing frost nips? While in the physical therapy gym, I developed a sense of appreciation for the machines specializing in the rehabilitations of arms, shoulders, back, legs, and even the hip. I felt captivated by every explanation from my physical therapist, the biomechanics of each movement and of each exercise. I craved the knowledge of these physicians, the capabilities of these devices, and how I could be a part of helping someone like me. At that moment, it became obvious: I wanted to be an engineer. I wanted to apply what I could do best, mathematics and problem solving, in the form of technological innovation for the advancements of medical accommodations. The idea of biomechanical engineering resonates strongly with my passion and interest in medical accessibility. A lot of low-income minority communities do not have access to affordable healthcare and therefore neglect their own health and wellbeing. Sicknesses can go unnoticed, contributing to the growing health gaps in minority communities. Besides my own struggles, I also grew up as a witness to my parents neglecting their doctor’s appointments, nutritional intake, and yearly checkups all in exchange for a more secure financial standing. Even then, I understand the privilege of having had access to amazing machinery and rehabilitation opportunities. But for those low-income and minority families who have no one to rely on, I can only imagine the crushing experience of living without any kind of healthcare. For many throughout the world, it is a reality. With the privilege of having access to an opportunity for an affordable higher education, I feel a sense of responsibility to represent my community and bring back my success in the form of accommodative support and health services. Knowing that college can be the catalyst for me to make an impact on low-income families like my own motivates my journey through learning more about the possibilities of engineering and medical innovation.

That night, as I lay awake, I decided I needed to act. Fueled by concern and her determination to live without limits, I spent weeks researching assistive devices. I discovered that existing tools like the walking cane lacked modern technological features to provide real-time data. My afternoons became consumed with designing and testing solutions. Having little to no experience with engineering at the time, I taught myself how to code, use microcontrollers, and solder. I overcame various obstacles including failed prototypes and unsuccessful designs as an engineering beginner. After months of research and countless trials and errors, I had created a device using an infrared sensor with visual, auditory, and tactile alerts. When objects were within a certain distance, the device would illuminate with an LED light, vibrate, and emit a buzzing sound, helping to alert her as she crossed busy intersections. The first time I watched her confidently cross the street was life-changing. As she crossed she utilized the invention to know when vehicles had passed, when pedestrians were approaching, and most importantly when it was safe to continue. Within college, I hope to expand my invention and create research projects aimed at uplifting individuals with disabilities. This experience and accomplishment was my first introduction to the world of engineering. It has empowered me to further explore engineering and has sparked my passion for empathy-driven innovation. More importantly, it has taught me that true fulfillment comes from making a tangible difference in someone's life. This is why I passionately want to pursue Biomedical Engineering and develop breakthroughs within the field of medicine and engineering.

column79: There it was in front of me, the RTX 2080 ti, illuminated in its display at my local Microcenter. I carefully gazed upon its silver casing, keeping my distance to make sure I couldn’t possibly damage the brilliant artifact. Its mesmerizing RGB lights twinkled in my adolescent eyes, but the price tag shined brighter. My family couldn’t possibly afford it, so I settled with just gawking at the computer component from a distance, silently planning for the day I could purchase one. I internalized the manufacturing processes, the release of new components, and news surrounding computer companies, preparing myself for the day I could finally afford one. I began to scour its large catalogue for computer parts, but was met with a frustrating revelation: affordable components are so poorly designed. Crucial features were cut from them, while superfluous aspects were prioritized (for example, motherboards would forgo M.2 slots, but include a VGA port released in 1987). I was forced to peruse their secondhand parts, the only ones I could realistically afford on account of their slightly discounted prices. Though I was ultimately successful in acquiring my own computer parts, I realized that my favorite hobby’s access was still extremely limited: inexpensive components are not made with the consumer in mind. Frustrated with my revelation, I dreamt of having my interest explored by others who are intrigued with it regardless of their background. A newfound aspiration was ignited in me inside of that Microcenter, as I realized I could make my passion more accessible to others. In my senior year of high school, I created an organization that would revitalize unused computer hardware and donate them to places with restricted availability to the internet: the Computer Refurbishing Club. I dream of creating my own innovative computer parts by studying computer engineering. Computer Engineering would arm me with the knowledge to create components that remove unutilized features while concentrating on attributes that go underappreciated by current computer hardware engineers. By creating components tailored to the consumers' needs, sold at an inexpensive price, I could rectify a bridge to my passion.

column79: I have always been fascinated by how things work, from the mechanics of everyday objects to the way our bodies function. This curiosity, combined with a desire to help others, led me to pursue a career in mechanical engineering, specifically in the field of medical devices and healthcare technology**. The intersection of engineering and medicine is where I see endless opportunities for innovation, and I am excited about the potential to make a tangible impact on improving lives through cutting-edge technologies. The healthcare industry is constantly evolving, and new challenges arise every day in patient care, treatment, and recovery. One area where mechanical engineering can contribute is in the development of medical devices such as prosthetics, diagnostic equipment, and surgical tools. My interest in this field was sparked by my volunteer experience at Lurie Children’s Hospital, where I saw firsthand the challenges young patients faced due to medical conditions. It made me realize how much technology, particularly mechanical devices, can improve their lives. Mechanical engineering equips individuals with the tools and knowledge necessary to design functional, efficient, and reliable medical devices. I will gain proficiency in key areas such as materials science, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, and robotics—skills essential for creating innovative solutions. For example, prosthetic devices need to be not only affordable but also comfortable, durable, lightweight, and customizable. I want to contribute to making prosthetics that allow individuals to regain mobility and improve their quality of life. I am also deeply interested in biomechanics, applying mechanical principles to biological systems. By studying how forces affect the human body, engineers can design assistive devices like exoskeletons or robotic limbs, technologies that restore mobility for individuals with disabilities. My goal is to improve these devices’ efficiency and accessibility. Mechanical engineers also play an essential role in improving healthcare systems. I am interested in optimizing manufacturing processes, improving accessibility, and enhancing how medical teams use technology. These innovations can help healthcare providers deliver faster, more accurate care, improving patient outcomes. An engineering education provides not only technical skills but also critical thinking, problem-solving, and teamwork abilities. By collaborating with doctors, healthcare providers, and other professionals, I will bridge the gap between engineering solutions and their practical application. column79: At fifteen, I sat on the sidelines, my ankle wrapped in ice, my mind tangled with frustration. The pain wasn’t just physical. It gnawed at something deeper. I had spent months recovering from a sprained wrist, only to return to the same spot on the bench. I felt powerless, like my body had betrayed me. The screech of sneakers on hardwood faded, dulling a world I could no longer reach. But as I sat there, frustration turned to fixation. I started noticing patterns: how certain players landed on one foot after rebounds or how some shoes buckled at sharp angles. Each movement felt like a puzzle piece hinting at disaster. I wanted to know if there was a way to predict these moments to stop injuries before they happened. That curiosity never left me. When I discovered AWS technology simulates NFL scenarios to predict injury risks, it felt like a door swinging open. Inspired, I dove into data science, attending a boot camp where I built a regression model to predict NBA standings. Analyzing shooting efficiency and turnover rates, I wrestled with numbers that refused to behave. When unexpected adjustments reduced accuracy, I realized data wasn’t just about equations; it was about context. Patterns reveal their meaning when you understand the stories behind them. As an adult, I see myself as a data scientist for the NBA, blending my love for sports and data to revolutionize athletic safety. I envision creating models that analyze biomechanics, court conditions, and fatigue levels to identify injury risks before they unfold. But my dream extends beyond numbers on a screen: I want to design a reimagined shoe and improved court surface that actively reduces injuries during games. Yet this journey isn’t just about innovation. I know what it’s like to sit in the shadows, powerless as the game moves on without you. Missing that season wasn’t just disappointing; it made me question my identity. Was I still an athlete if I couldn’t play? I watched teammates grow stronger while I spent practices staring at the floor, dreading the coach’s gaze. But that time off also gave me perspective. I realized that my love for basketball wasn’t defined by how often I played, but by my desire to improve the game. That realization transformed my frustration into focus. I push myself to uncover patterns others might overlook and am determined to make an impact. Because I know the heartbreak of seeing a dream slip away, I want to ensure fewer athletes experience that same helplessness. I want to build a future where players step onto the court, knowing the game they love won’t betray them. One day, I won’t just be watching those moments unfold. I’ll know I played a role in preserving them because the game-winning shots, the no-look passes, and the impossible comebacks deserve to happen without fear. And if I can use data to make those moments safer, I’ll know I’ve done more than predict the future. I’ll have helped change it.
